newsitem.title: FRANCE: Poll throws French snap election race wide open.
newsitem.headline: Poll throws French snap election race wide open.

text.p: An opinion poll threw France's snap election race wide open on Thursday, predicting only a wafer-thin parliamentary majority for the centre-right government.

The government ordered a public spending freeze for 1998 as another survey showed many voters feel a single European currency will threaten jobs and economic growth. The opposition Socialists wooed voters with a pledge of no new taxes.

An IPSOS poll for the weekly Le Point showed the ruling coalition would win 292 seats in the 577-member National Assembly, with the opposition Socialists taking 256, the Communists 28 and the far-right National Front 1 in the May 25-June 1 election.
Thirty-one percent of those questioned did not state their voting intention. The poll was taken on Tuesday and Wednesday, after President Jacques Chirac called the election on Monday.

Prime Minister Alain Juppe's office confirmed that ministers had been told to hold 1998 state spending unchanged in nominal terms for the second successive year, meaning a cut of more than one percent in real terms.
But it sought to offset the impression of austerity by trumpeting signs of an economic upturn ahead of the election, likely to be dominated by the issues of unemployment, taxes and purchasing power.

"Growth is taking off again," Budget Minister Alain Lamassoure said, pointing to what he called robust industrial production figures. He said France might make more tax cuts than planned if economic growth exceeded forecasts for 1997.
A Louis Harris survey for Valeurs Actuelles magazine showed that most voters believed there were alternatives to the government's economic policies meant to prepare for the single currency from 1999.

And 69 percent of those quizzed favoured a new referendum on the introduction of the euro currency. Voters narrowly approved the Maastricht Treaty on European union, including the currency, in a 1992 referendum.
The Harris survey, taken before Chirac announced the election, showed 50 percent reckoned the single currency would fail to help "a return to economic growth", while 43 percent felt it could succeed.
Seventy-three percent of the 951 people surveyed believed the euro would not help cut unemployment in major European nations, with just 20 percent saying it would.

The Socialists, who say they favour the euro but not at the price of a further bout of austerity, accused the conservatives of trying to secure re-election before imposing draconian new austerity to help qualify for the single European currency.

"We will not raise taxes," Martine Aubry, a member of the Socialist leadership, said in an RTL radio interview. "We will simply make a better share-out between (taxes on) income from capital and income from salaries, we will relaunch consumer spending and introduce a new model of development," she said.
The ruling coalition partners said at a joint leadership meeting chaired by the RPR's Juppe and the UDF's Francois Leotard that their common manifesto should be ready on Monday.

In their first meetings with ordinary voters since the campaign kicked off, Juppe was to travel to the rough and tumble Mediterranean port of Marseille, while Socialist leader Lionel Jospin planned to tour several troubled outer Paris suburbs.
Far-right leader Jean-Marie Le Pen said he hoped his National Front party would win 20 seats, enough for it to form its own parliamentary group. It now has no seats.

Private television channel TF1 invited the leaders of the four biggest parties -- the RPR, UDF, Socialists and Communists -- to a live debate on May 20. Juppe and Jospin have already said they would welcome a face-to-face debate.

In a reminder of nagging labour unrest since unions brought France to a virtual standstill for 24 days in late 1995 to protest at government policies, a one-day strike by train conductors over wage demands cut rail services to about a third of normal in many parts of France.
